newsitem.title: GERMANY: Aznar in Bonn to push Spain's EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: Aznar in Bonn to push Spain's EMU entry.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar arrived in Bonn on Thursday for consultations certain to focus on Madrid's determination to join the EU single currency at the outset, despite reservations being expressed in Germany.

Aznar left no doubt in an interview in the weekly Die Zeit that he expected Spain to meet the qualification criteria this year to join European Monetary Union (EMU), and to be admitted in 1999 on merit.
"I would stake everything I have on that," he said. "I don't have the slightest doubt that we will make it."

Spanish delegation sources say Aznar and his ministers have come armed with evidence of their young government's economic accomplishments and hoping for acknowledgement from Bonn that they are on course to join the first wave of EMU entrants.

But as the deadline for EMU approaches, northern Europeans have begun to worry that countries such as Italy or Spain may have invested too much political capital in joining EMU before their economies are geared to long-term stability.

Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm has spoken of single currency "hysteria" in southern Europe. On Tuesday German Finance Ministry number two Juergen Stark made clear that the well-documented worries of Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer were also shared in Bonn.

While Madrid has garnered popular support for its EMU drive with the carrot of joining the EU elite on equal terms, Bonn has to calm Germans' fears that they may end up baling out the deficits of countries less committed to budget discipline.

Stark did not name any countries, but there was little doubt he was aiming at southern European EU members when he told a conference of newspaper editors that even some countries who qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibilty for a certain period".
"Do (the Germans) really think we Spanish want a weak currency? We want exactly what the Germans want: a strong euro."

Both Aznar and Spanish Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato, in remarks to industrialists in Bonn on Wednesday, made clear they expected Spain's entry to be judged strictly according to the entry criteria in the Maastricht Treaty, and nothing else.

The Spanish government also argues that it has put in place a number of reforms which provide evidence of its commitment to long-term stability, including strict budgetary rules which prevent the circumvention of public spending limits and a domestic stability pact between central government and regions.

Aznar was accompanied by 11 cabinet ministers covering the portfolios of the economy, foreign affairs, justice, defence, home affairs, development, education, labour, industry, agriculture and the environment.

One major topic on the agenda is certain to be Spanish fears of losing out as the countries who are net contributors to the EU budget, including Germany, seek to reduce payments to EU structural funds ahead of the planned admission of east European countries.
